transcript.text: Hello, everyone, and welcome to Greenfield Recycling Centre. My name's Mr Bell, and I'm the manager here. Before we begin the tour, I'll explain how the site is arranged, so please look at the plan in front of you.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: We deal with about two hundred tonnes of waste every week, and more than half of it is recycled, which is much better than five years ago. That is thanks to the people who bring their rubbish here already sorted.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: You came in through the main gate at the bottom of the plan. Straight ahead of you is the car park, which is in the middle of the site. Please leave your cars there if you are visiting, and never drive past it.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: Just inside the gate, on your left, is the reception office. That's where you sign in and collect a yellow jacket. You must wear it at all times on site.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: Opposite the reception office, on the right, there's a small café. It's open from eight until four, and the coffee is cheap, so I recommend it after the tour.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: Now, walk with me along the left side of the car park. Halfway along, beside the fence, you'll see the clothes bank. People bring old jackets and shoes here, and a charity collects them every Tuesday.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: At the far left corner, at the back of the site, is the glass area. We have three different containers, one for each colour: clear, green and brown. Please don't mix the colours, because it makes the recycling more difficult.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: Next to it, in the middle at the back, is the electronics area. Old phones, kettles and computers go there. Please don't throw them in the ordinary bins, because they contain metals that can harm the environment.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: The garden waste is in the back right corner. We turn this into compost, which local people can buy cheaply in the spring.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: We sell the compost at a very low price because we want people to use it, and it's much better for the garden than the bags you buy in the supermarket.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: On the right side in the middle of the site is the metal area, but we won't visit it today, because it's closed for repairs until the end of the month. I know some of you are disappointed, but we'll look at photographs on the way back.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: Now a few practical points. First, how much does it cost? For ordinary household items, nothing at all. But if you bring building materials, such as bricks or tiles, there's a small charge of six pounds per bag.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: Second, opening hours. We're open every day except Wednesday, from eight in the morning until five in the afternoon, although in winter we close at four because it gets dark early.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: Third, safety. Children are very welcome, but they must stay with an adult all the time. The heavy lorries move around the site, and the drivers can't always see small people.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: Finally, volunteers. We're looking for people to help on Saturday mornings, especially to explain the different bins to visitors. You don't need any experience, just a friendly attitude.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: Last year our volunteers also organised a school visit, and a whole class of children came to learn how rubbish is sorted. They were surprisingly enthusiastic.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL

transcript.text: Right, if there are no questions, let's start the tour. Please follow me, and stay together.
transcript.speaker: MR BELL
